name: Tomas Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. We do not sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the brass section at a small theatre, teach trumpet on Tuesdays, and record short demos for local shows when somebody calls. My music master’s helps in rehearsal, but the invoices and late buses are part of the day too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment four players breathe together before the first note. I do not like counting missed lessons against the food bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the brass section that AI can tidy the booking email, but somebody still has to breathe at the same time onstage. My students would laugh if I called that a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I am less relaxed about the ordinary bills. I lead the section at a small theatre, but my pay is low and my account would not carry a full month without lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the theatre rehearsals and Tuesday trumpet pupils. This winter I will use the calendar tool I already know for lesson reminders, then put any missed-cancellation fee toward the rent buffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel mostly steady about the technology, but uneasy about a thin month. My best playing cannot stretch a bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which small task could the software actually help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One parent forgot the Tuesday lesson twice last month. A reminder might save a slot, though I will call if the message is missed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the theatre manager to leave with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre manager to keep the section roster human. Software can put dates in boxes; it cannot tell when a player is too tired to take a solo.

say: I would say **booking reminders** may improve without changing what brass players do onstage.
I would ask the manager to keep the **section roster** with musicians.
think: My **low pay** and nearly empty account are the real risks in a slow month.
Missed **lesson fees** matter more than a new calendar tool.
do: Keep **theatre rehearsals** and Tuesday trumpet pupils on the same weekly schedule this winter.
Use **lesson reminders** to reduce missed Tuesday slots.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about my bank balance, though the technology seems manageable.
S0.quote: My best playing cannot stretch a bank balance.
fieldNote: His lead role does not remove the **low pay** or narrow local job market.
He uses a proven **calendar tool** but keeps personal contact when a family misses a message.

steps.text: Keep theatre brass rehearsals and Tuesday trumpet lessons

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the theatre can use AI for posters, bookings and draft scores, but the section needs a person to lead rehearsal. I would ask management to show us where the saved money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the quick studio demos I record for local shows would dry up. I also fear the theatre may leave a vacant chair empty and ask the rest of us to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next week I would ask the players committee for the theatre budget and join its meeting. In the first year I would learn the approved score-checking tool from our sound technician, but only use it after checking every part by ear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the missing demo fees and extra rehearsals. It would still feel like I had a say if the players could see the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the lost demo fee change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The demo money pays for food in thin teaching weeks, not treats. I would stop counting it in next term’s budget as soon as clients switch, and cut the takeaway after late rehearsals to save about 20 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust a machine score in rehearsal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I will not take a software score straight to the players. If the trumpet line sits out of range, I own that mistake as section lead.

say: I would ask management to show where **AI savings** go when bookings and scores change.
I would defend a **human section lead** in rehearsal.
think: My **studio demos** may lose buyers as software can draft music cheaply.
The theatre might leave a **vacant chair** empty and stretch the remaining players.
do: Join the **players committee** meeting and ask for the theatre budget next week.
Learn the approved **score tool**, using generated parts only after checking every part by ear.
Cut the **weekly takeaway** after late rehearsals if demo clients switch.
feel: I feel **anxious** about food money and extra work, though the committee gives me a voice.
S1.quote: The demo money pays for food in thin teaching weeks, not treats.
fieldNote: He sees **demo fees** as basic household income, rather than disposable money.
His cautious **tool use** fits his steady adaptability and senior responsibility for the brass section.

steps.text: Join the theatre players committee budget meeting
Learn approved score checking; check every part by ear before use
Cut the 20 weekly takeaway if demo clients switch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players that AGI by 2028 can make the drafts and bookings, but our live sound has to be valued. I would ask for written terms before any shorter season is announced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my demo and arranging fees to go in 2028, and perhaps the theatre cuts paid rehearsal hours then. Robots arrive around 2031 in this picture, so the stage chairs have a little longer, but that does not pay for the lost work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would collect my theatre and teaching contracts and call the players committee chair. If the 2028 cuts come, I would check community school vacancies, apply for a second teaching post if one is advertised, and ask the association about temporary income help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed. There are few posts like mine nearby, and I do not have the savings to make a long search comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut before touching instrument insurance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cut the paid rehearsal room first, about 70 a month, and practise at home during permitted hours. I would keep the instrument insurance because one dent would take a week of lessons to repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner that you might not tell the players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could talk confidently to the brass section, but I would tell my partner that I am scared of the rent date. Being section lead would not protect a cancelled season.

say: I would demand **written terms** before the theatre shortens a season.
I would say live **brass sound** still deserves a paid chair.
think: My **demo fees** could vanish in 2028 before stage robots appear around 2031.
A cancelled **theatre season** would defeat my senior title and thin savings.
do: Gather **contracts** and speak with the players committee chair this month.
Check **school vacancies** if 2028 cuts arrive, applying for advertised posts and asking the association about income help.
Cancel the **70 monthly rehearsal room** if cuts arrive in 2028, while keeping instrument insurance.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a rent date that cannot wait for a new job.
S2.quote: Being section lead would not protect a cancelled season.
fieldNote: He clearly distinguishes **2028 thinking work** losses from the later 2031 robot risk.
His private **rent fear** is sharper than the firm public position he would take with players.

steps.text: Ask the players committee chair for written season terms
Apply for advertised community school teaching posts if 2028 cuts arrive
Ask association about income help if 2028 cuts arrive
Cancel the 70 monthly rehearsal room if 2028 cuts arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the section that five years is enough time to negotiate a different season and teach more pupils. I would not tell a new student to stop learning an instrument because a machine can write music.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect the theatre will use AGI in 2031 to shrink its paid arranging work. Stage robots around 2034 are possible, but the audience might still want living players; I would rather have a second income before testing that belief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the community school this spring whether its adult evening class has room for a trumpet teacher. If they offer a term, I would teach it alongside the theatre, save half that extra pay, and continue through the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but less boxed in than in the fast picture. Five years gives me time to see whether the evening class fills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many students would replace your demo money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A class of eight paying adults would cover the missing demo fees. If only three enrol, I would keep the theatre hours and try again next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep using the score tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still use the score tool for checking ranges, after hearing the notes myself. I can accept a second check without asking a machine to be the conductor.

say: I would tell players we have **five years** to bargain and add teaching hours.
I would encourage new students to keep **learning instruments**.
think: Paid **arranging work** may shrink in 2031, before possible stage robots around 2034.
I want a **second income** before I learn whether audiences still pay for human players.
do: Ask the **community school** this spring about its adult evening class.
Save half the **extra class pay** if a full term is offered.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but a five-year window lets me test enrollment.
S3.quote: I can accept a second check without asking a machine to be the conductor.
fieldNote: He chooses an **adjacent teaching role**, which uses his music degree and avoids a sudden career switch.
The plan depends on **eight paying adults**, and he says what happens if only three enroll.

steps.text: Teach adult trumpet class if offered, continuing through the year after 2031
Save half the extra class pay if a full term runs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the brass section that ten years lets us make a case for live players and train younger ones. I would ask the theatre to put an apprenticeship line in its next season plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I hope my evening class could replace the demo work, but I cannot promise that today. Robots around 2039 might play the notes; what people pay to hear is still an open question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start a yearly record of paid theatre and lesson hours now and take it to the players committee each spring. If the evening class fills, I would save part of its pay, and in the first year after 2036 I would compare actual theatre bookings with that record before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the next thin teaching month, even with ten years to prepare. The theatre could cut a season for ordinary budget reasons tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the yearly record do for the players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The record would show whether hours disappear one season at a time. I want our committee to bargain from pay slips, not guesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a younger musician to prepare?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my younger pupil to learn to listen to another player and also to read a contract. A machine may play a note; it cannot promise a fair wage.

say: I would ask the theatre to fund a **young player apprenticeship** in its next season.
I would tell players to bargain from **paid hours**, not guesses.
think: A filled **evening class** might replace demo income by 2036, but enrollment is uncertain.
Even before 2039 robots, an ordinary **theatre budget cut** remains possible.
do: Record **paid hours** from theatre and lessons each season starting now.
Compare **actual bookings** with that record in the first year after 2036.
Save part of **evening class pay** if enough adults enroll.
feel: I feel **anxious** about thin months because ten years does not secure the next season.
S4.quote: I want our committee to bargain from pay slips, not guesses.
fieldNote: His **ten-year plan** is evidence gathering and a teaching income he can test.
He remains **anxious** because present theatre budgets can cut hours before any AGI deadline.

steps.text: Take a yearly paid-hours record to the players committee
Save part of evening class pay if enrollment fills
Compare 2036 theatre bookings with earlier paid hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest one, because I could lose demos and paid rehearsals before finding more pupils. A written season agreement, temporary income help and a school teaching opening would make a real difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a young player can afford the first three unpaid years people keep calling experience. The orchestra loses talent long before a robot takes a chair.

headlineQuote: The orchestra loses talent long before a robot takes a chair.
portrait: At **27**, Tomas leads a theatre brass section, teaches trumpet and records demos despite low pay and scant savings.
He uses **proven tools** cautiously, checking machine scores by ear and keeping people responsible for rehearsal decisions.
His **players committee** gives him a way to demand contracts and track paid hours as thinking work changes.
He tests an **adult class** as a second income, saving only if enrollment supports a full term.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove demo fees and paid rehearsals before Tomas secures a second teaching post.
whatWouldHelp: A **written season agreement**, temporary income help and a school teaching opening would bridge the transition.
